bib.title: Chapter 2: Understanding Large Language Models (Generative AI and LLMs For Dummies, Snowflake Special Edition)
bib.venue: John Wiley & Sons, Inc. (For Dummies, Snowflake Special Edition); authors not printed in this chapter

question: What kinds of LLMs exist, what technology powers them, and how should an enterprise handle vectors, tooling and data governance?
contributions: Categorises LLMs as general-purpose, task-specific, domain-specific and foundation models
Defines prompt, completion, inference, embeddings, vector databases
Lists developer frameworks and argues for governing data inside a cloud data platform

limits: Vendor-sponsored (Snowflake Special Edition); promotes a cloud data platform and Snowflake Cortex/Copilot.
Dated: refers to Google Bard, GPT-3/3.5/4, Llama 2 and Bing as current (2024 print).

Some claims are loose or wrong: BERT is said to power Bard (Bard ran on LaMDA/PaLM); CodeBERT is called a cybersecurity solution (it is a code/natural-language model); BioBERT is attributed to NVIDIA (it came from Korea University/DMIS, though NVIDIA released a BioBERT checkpoint); XLNet described as for multilingual translation; BERT, XLNet etc. are not generative LLMs in the GPT sense. These corrections come from outside the PDF and are the reader's note, not the chapter's.
Says vector embeddings are 'the most efficient way' to store language with no evidence.
No numbers beyond one market forecast; no architecture, training or evaluation detail.
practices: Include vector search (RAG, ICL, vector similarity search) in the data platform for gen AI work (p.16).
Bring processing to the data rather than data to the processing engine, so prompts and completions stay within governed access (p.17).
Apply governance across structured, semistructured and unstructured data; object stores lack row-level permissions (p.18).
Build user interfaces so users can interact with LLMs in designated ways to drive adoption (p.14).
